It successfully blends classic **Agatha Christie-style country house mystery** elements with a high-concept speculative mechanism. |

***

### Part 2: Structured Summary of Plot and Central Conceit

The novel centers on **Aiden Bishop**, who awakens at Blackheath manor with no memory of who he is. He is informed by mysterious figures that he is trapped in a decaying time loop and that he must solve the murder of **Evelyn Hardcastle** before midnight. If he fails, the day will reset, and he will awaken to inhabit a different host.

| Element | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Central Conceit** | **Body-Hopping Time Loop.** The protagonist must solve a murder by reliving the same day, **November 8, 1933**, repeatedly. |
| **The "Hosts"** | Over the course of the game, Aiden will inhabit the body of **eight different guests** staying at the manor. Each host dies at a set time, meaning Aiden has limited time in each body. |
| **The Goal** | Identify Evelyn Hardcastle's killer and successfully prevent her murder before the loop ends permanently (or before he runs out of hosts). |
| **The Mechanism of Progression** | Progress is tied to **Perspective and Knowledge**. Each host offers different physical capabilities, social access, and crucial pieces of information. Solving the mystery is not just about finding clues but about viewing the day from mutually exclusive viewpoints to piece together the truth. |
| **Narrative Structure** | **Cyclical and Non-Linear within a Finite Set.** The structure is highly experimental because the protagonist's understanding of the day evolves across discrete, repeated cycles, forcing the reader to re-evaluate events based on the new perspective inhabiting the current body. |

{"result": {"title": "The Seven Deaths of Evelyn Hardcastle", "author": "Stuart Turton", "year": 2018, "word_count": 116000, "text": "Day One.

I remember running. I remember the sound of my own breathing, ragged with panic, and the damp cold of the air against my face. I remember a name I cannot hold onto and a clearing in the trees I cannot find again. I remember screaming for someone called Anna, and Anna not coming. That is all I remember, and when I try to hold any of it for longer than a moment it slides out of reach, like a smooth stone sliding down a muddy bank.

I find that I am standing at the edge of a wood. Mist clings to the lower branches; the trunks disappear upward into grey. Somewhere behind me a rook calls twice and stops. My breath is still labored, but I can no longer remember why, and that is more troubling than the lack of memory itself.

There is a man beside me. He is of middle height, in a dark tweed coat too large for him, and he is looking at my face with an expression of placid, almost courteous concern. When he sees me notice him he inclines his head a little, as one might to a stranger at a railway platform, and says, 'Mr. Ashton, I think the best thing now is to walk back to the house.'

Mr. Ashton. He means me. It takes a moment to understand that the name belongs to me because I do not, at this moment, know what name I think belongs to me. I try the word in my mouth silently and it sits there without meaning. Ashton. Edward Ashton? No, that isn't right either. I have the distinct sense that I am not Mr. Ashton at all, but that I am supposed to be, and that the man beside me believes without question that I am.", "source": "library-service"}, "error": null}
